mcqs.q: Osteomyelitis is defined as:
opts: Inflammation of bone and marrow, almost always secondary to infection
mcqs.explain: Osteomyelitis denotes inflammation of bone and marrow, almost always secondary to infection.

mcqs.q: The MOST common causative organism of acute pyogenic osteomyelitis is:
mcqs.explain: Staphylococcus aureus causes about 80% of acute pyogenic osteomyelitis.

mcqs.q: Osteomyelitis caused by Salmonella is classically associated with:
mcqs.explain: Salmonella osteomyelitis is characteristically seen in patients with sickle-cell anaemia.

mcqs.q: In NEONATES, osteomyelitis is commonly caused by:
opts: Haemophilus influenzae or group B streptococci
mcqs.explain: Haemophilus influenzae and group B streptococci are common causes in neonates.

mcqs.q: The site of osteomyelitis is determined by the bone's vascular supply; in OLDER children and adults the infection localises to the:
mcqs.explain: In older children/adults the plate is closed, so infection localises to the metaphysis (vascular loop with sluggish flow); in infants <2 y, trans-epiphyseal vessels let bacteria reach the epiphysis.

mcqs.q: Why is the metaphysis a common site of osteomyelitis?
opts: Its vascular loops have sluggish blood flow that traps bacteria
mcqs.explain: The metaphysis has hairpin vascular loops with sluggish flow, favouring bacterial lodgement.

mcqs.q: Bacteria reach the bone in osteomyelitis via:
opts: The bloodstream, a compound fracture, or a skin/soft-tissue infection
mcqs.explain: Routes of infection are haematogenous (bloodstream), a compound (open) fracture, or contiguous spread from skin/soft-tissue infection.

mcqs.q: In acute osteomyelitis, dead (ischaemic-necrotic) bone is called the:
mcqs.explain: A sequestrum is a fragment of dead (necrotic) bone produced by ischaemia in acute osteomyelitis.

mcqs.q: The reactive NEW bone that forms around the dead bone is the:
mcqs.explain: The involucrum is the sheath of reactive new bone that forms around the sequestrum.

mcqs.q: The external opening through which pus drains from the bone is the:
mcqs.explain: The cloaca is the opening of the draining sinus through which pus escapes to the surface.

mcqs.q: The sequence in acute osteomyelitis is suppuration →:
opts: Abscess → elevated periosteum → ischaemic necrosis (sequestrum) and new bone (involucrum)
mcqs.explain: Suppuration forms an abscess that elevates the periosteum, causing ischaemic necrosis (sequestrum) and reactive new bone (involucrum).

mcqs.q: Chronic sclerosing non-suppurative osteomyelitis (Garré) shows which radiological appearance?
mcqs.explain: Garré's sclerosing osteomyelitis shows bone sclerosis/thickening with an 'onion-skin' periosteal appearance and no suppuration.

mcqs.q: Brodie's abscess is classically a:
opts: Subacute/chronic 1–4 cm bone abscess with a fibrous wall, in the metaphysis of the tibia in children
Diffuse acute infection of the whole bone
mcqs.explain: Brodie's abscess is a subacute/chronic 1–4 cm bone abscess with a fibrous wall and surrounding sclerosis, typically in the metaphysis of the tibia in children.

mcqs.q: Vertebral acute osteomyelitis typically:
opts: Starts as disc infection (discitis) and spreads to adjacent vertebral bodies, usually without collapse
mcqs.explain: Vertebral OM starts as discitis; pus extends to the adjacent vertebral bodies, usually without vertebral collapse or disc prolapse.

mcqs.q: Acute osteomyelitis is more common in children and presents with:
opts: Fever, pain, swelling, redness, heat and sinus formation
mcqs.explain: Acute OM (commoner in children) causes local fever, pain, swelling, redness, heat and sinus formation, plus general malaise, weight loss and anorexia.

mcqs.q: A complication of acute osteomyelitis is:
mcqs.explain: Complications include osteonecrosis (ischaemic bone death), septicaemia, metastatic abscesses and progression to chronic OM.

mcqs.q: The predominant inflammatory cell in ACUTE pyogenic osteomyelitis is the:
mcqs.explain: Acute (pyogenic) osteomyelitis is an acute inflammation dominated by neutrophils, with pus formation.

mcqs.q: In INFANTS (<2 years), osteomyelitis is especially dangerous because:
opts: Trans-epiphyseal vessels are open, allowing infection to reach the epiphysis (and joint)
mcqs.explain: In infants the growth plate is not a barrier — open trans-epiphyseal vessels let infection spread to the epiphysis and joint.

mcqs.q: Coliform organisms cause osteomyelitis particularly in:
opts: Patients with urinary-tract infection or IV drug use
mcqs.explain: Coliforms are implicated in osteomyelitis in patients with UTI and in IV drug users.

mcqs.q: Mixed-organism osteomyelitis is most typical of:
mcqs.explain: Mixed (polymicrobial) osteomyelitis usually follows trauma/open wounds.

mcqs.q: Tuberculous osteomyelitis is classified as a form of:
mcqs.explain: TB osteomyelitis is a chronic specific (granulomatous) osteomyelitis; the chronic group also includes non-specific forms.

mcqs.q: The dead bone in a sequestrum results from:
opts: Ischaemic necrosis after the abscess compresses/strips the periosteal blood supply
mcqs.explain: Pus elevating the periosteum strips the blood supply, causing ischaemic necrosis of the bone — the sequestrum.

saqs.a: Inflammation of bone and marrow, almost always secondary to infection. Types: acute (pyogenic) and chronic (non-specific or tuberculous).

saqs.q: Match the organism to its clinical setting (Staph aureus, Salmonella, neonatal).
saqs.a: Staph aureus — commonest (80%); Salmonella — sickle-cell anaemia; H. influenzae/GBS — neonates.

saqs.q: Explain why the metaphysis is the common site and why infant OM is dangerous.
saqs.a: The metaphysis has sluggish vascular loops that trap bacteria. In infants, open trans-epiphyseal vessels let infection reach the epiphysis and joint.
Sequestrum = dead (necrotic) bone. Involucrum = reactive new bone around it. Cloaca = the draining-sinus opening.

saqs.q: Describe Garré's sclerosing OM and Brodie's abscess.
saqs.a: Garré: non-suppurative sclerosis, 'onion-skin' thickening, children. Brodie's abscess: subacute 1–4 cm bone abscess with fibrous wall, in the tibial metaphysis.

saqs.q: Describe the pathology sequence of acute osteomyelitis.
saqs.a: Suppuration → abscess → elevated periosteum → ischaemic necrosis (sequestrum) + reactive new bone (involucrum) → draining sinus (cloaca).

saqs.q: List the clinical features and complications of acute osteomyelitis.
saqs.a: Features: fever, pain, swelling, redness, heat, sinus (commoner in children). Complications: osteonecrosis, septicaemia, metastatic abscesses.
